title: Ranking & Hybrid Recommenders
summary: The practical multi-stage pipeline production recommenders actually run — candidate generation, ranking, hybrid signals, and honest evaluation.

slides.markdown:
No production recommender scores the whole catalog with one expensive model — it's a **funnel**: a cheap **candidate generation** stage (often a two-tower model, see [deep-learning-recommenders](deep-learning-recommenders)) cuts millions of items down to a few hundred, then a much more expensive **ranking** model, using rich features and full cross-feature interactions, scores just that shortlist precisely.

This split exists purely for latency and cost: the ranking model can afford to be slow-but-accurate because it only ever runs on a few hundred candidates, not the whole catalog.

A **hybrid recommender** blends content-based and collaborative signal rather than picking one, because each covers the other's blind spot: content-based features handle new items, collaborative signal captures taste patterns no feature could encode.

The blend can happen at different points — as separate scores combined by a weighted sum, as separate candidate sets merged before ranking, or (most common today) as just more input features fed into one ranking model that learns the right weighting itself rather than having it hand-tuned.

The final ranking stage is usually a **learning-to-rank** model — trained not to predict an absolute score, but to get the *relative order* of candidates right. There are three families:

- **Pointwise** — predict a score per item independently (e.g. predicted click probability), then sort.
- **Pairwise** — learn from pairs, optimizing "item A should rank above item B."
- **Listwise** — optimize the whole ranked list's quality directly (e.g. against NDCG).

Most production rankers are pointwise in practice (simpler, cheaper, easy to calibrate against a real probability) even though pairwise/listwise better match the true ranking objective — see [evaluation-metrics-regression-ranking](evaluation-metrics-regression-ranking) for NDCG/MAP.

Pure relevance ranking, taken to its logical end, shows every user their single most-predicted-to-engage item ten times in a row — technically "correct," and a terrible product experience. Real systems explicitly optimize for **diversity** (don't show five near-identical items back to back) and **novelty** (surface things outside the user's obvious comfort zone occasionally).

This is usually done as a re-ranking step *after* the relevance model scores candidates — penalize near-duplicates, inject a small quota of exploratory items — rather than baking diversity into the relevance model itself, which is hard to do cleanly.

| | Offline | Online |
|---|---|---|
| Metrics | NDCG, precision@k, recall@k | CTR, watch-time, conversion, A/B-tested revenue |
| Speed | Fast, cheap, no user risk | Slow, needs real traffic, real risk |
| What it catches | "Does this model rank held-out data well?" | "Do real users actually behave differently because of it?" |

**How to decide:** offline metrics are a cheap first filter to reject clearly worse models before they ever see a real user; only online A/B tests can confirm the model actually moves the business metric you care about — offline and online rankings frequently disagree.

Optimizing purely for **click-through rate** teaches the ranker exactly what you asked it to: maximize clicks. It has no built-in notion of whether the click led anywhere good. The result is a system that gradually promotes misleading thumbnails, sensational headlines, and outrage-bait — content optimized to be clicked, not content optimized to be *valuable*.

The fix is choosing a label further downstream than the click itself — watch-time completion, post-click satisfaction surveys, return-visit rate — so the training signal actually correlates with the outcome you want, not just the easiest-to-game proxy for it.

A real production recommender, end to end: multiple **candidate generation** sources (collaborative two-tower, content-based, trending/popularity) merge into a shortlist of a few hundred; a **ranking** model scores that shortlist with rich features; a final **re-ranking** pass applies business rules (diversity, freshness, de-duping, policy filters) before anything hits the screen.

This exact pipeline shape reappears across feed ranking, search, and e-commerce recommendations — see [design-a-recommendation-system-e2e](design-a-recommendation-system-e2e) for the full interview case study.
